article_title: Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications
citation: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications and AI system design principles. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10655-6
title: The Productive Failure framework: two phases of generation/exploration and consolidation/knowledge assembly
description: The article presents a PF framework, extended from Kapur's two-phase model, organizing productive failure into two phases with six subcategories. Phase 1 covers problem exploration, solution generation, and collaborative problem-solving; Phase 2 covers comparison and contrast, knowledge reorganization, and knowledge transfer. The authors state, "The PF model is organized into two phases: (1) Generation and Exploration and (2) Consolidation and Knowledge Assembly." The framework structures both the course design and the thematic analysis of AI support.
requirements: Learners engage with complex, ill-structured problems targeting concepts they have not yet learned before receiving instruction
constraints: The authors note PF is not universally effective and depends on careful implementation, requiring a safe environment, skilled facilitation, and well-chosen problem content
target_learners: adult learners (typically 25 years or older) in higher education
target_learning_goals: deep understanding and long-term knowledge transfer through learning from initial failed attempts
examples: The 15-week COIL course structured team design work by PF phases, from initial brainstorming notes in Weeks 1-2 to final project reports in Weeks 13-15
key_sources: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications and AI system design principles. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10655-6

article_title: Preparatory effects of problem solving versus studying examples prior to instruction
citation: Christian Hartmann, Tamara van Gog, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Preparatory effects of problem solving versus studying examples prior to instruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09528-z
title: Preparatory mechanisms account for problem solving prior to instruction (prior knowledge activation, awareness of knowledge gaps, deep feature recognition)
description: The article works within the PF account that attempting (or observing) failed problem solving before instruction prepares learners through three mechanisms: "prior knowledge activation, awareness of knowledge gaps, and deep feature recognition". Activated incomplete schemas help learners integrate new conceptual knowledge during subsequent instruction, and awareness of gaps should make instruction more effective. The study tested these mechanisms against a vicarious-failure alternative and found the mechanism evidence mixed.
requirements: Learners must attempt or observe solution attempts on a complex but not ill-defined problem before receiving instruction on the canonical solution
constraints: The article states it had no direct measure of prior knowledge activation in all conditions, so the activation explanation remains speculative
The knowledge gap awareness items are described as rather unspecific, not assessing explicit knowledge about why a solution attempt failed
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of statistical variance concepts
examples: Students generated or observed failed solution attempts on a soccer cover-story task about variance before receiving instruction on mean absolute deviation
key_sources: Christian Hartmann, Tamara van Gog, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Preparatory effects of problem solving versus studying examples prior to instruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09528-z

article_title: Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement
citation: Cancela J, Burgo H, Sande E. (2019). Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 31: 556–562. https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jpts/31/7/31_17-478/_article
title: Physical fitness and executive function assessment battery for adolescents
description: A battery of nine physical tests and five cognitive instruments used to assess adolescents' fitness and executive functions: "resistance strength with the 30-second Chair Stand Test", explosive strength (standing broad jump), agility and speed (10 × 5 m shuttle run, quadrant jump), aerobic endurance (20 m shuttle run, 6 min endurance run), balance (BOT-2), flexibility (Sit and Reach, Back Scratch), plus PAQ-A, Stroop Golden Test, Wechsler Memory Scale, Symbol Digit Modalities Test, Trail Making Test and MESSY Scale. Academic achievement came from school records across six subjects scored 0–10.
requirements: Trained professionals administered the tests over a 5-month period in five randomly selected centers
constraints: Administered to Compulsory Secondary Education students in the Galician Autonomous Community
target_learning_goals: physical fitness and executive function assessment
examples: Data were collected with objective measurements and questionnaires by five trained education professionals
key_sources: Cancela J, Burgo H, Sande E. (2019). Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 31: 556–562. https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jpts/31/7/31_17-478/_article

article_title: When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains
citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Productive Failure: design features and three hypothesized learning mechanisms
description: Productive Failure combines two successive phases: an initial phase in which students collaboratively invent solution ideas for a complex novel problem without instructional support, and a delayed instruction phase in which the instructor builds on erroneous student solutions. The article states the design features "are expected to trigger the following three learning-related mechanisms which are hypothesized to underlie the effectiveness of PF (Loibl et al. 2017): (1) activation of prior knowledge, (2) awareness of knowledge limitations, and (3) recognition of the deep features of the targeted learning concepts." It applies this framework to design and evaluate a non-STEM instantiation of PF.
requirements: The problem must meet a sweet spot of complexity, addressing prior knowledge related to the targeted concept while students cannot solve it canonically
The delayed instruction must build on students' erroneous solution ideas, comparing and contrasting them with components of the canonical solution
constraints: The targeted concept needs a canonical solution with clearly definable components that can be compared with erroneous ideas, per the article's own argument
target_learners: secondary school students (10th graders in the studies)
target_learning_goals: acquisition of conceptual knowledge of the targeted learning topic
examples: In the two studies, PF students invented solution ideas for a teacher-conference study-design problem before receiving instruction that contrasted four typical error features with the canonical 2 × 2 factorial design.
key_sources: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2

article_title: Investigating students’ perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study
citation: Valentina Nachtigall, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Investigating students' perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09556-3
title: Productive Failure problem-solving phase structured by four design principles (problem/task, activity, participation structure, social surround)
description: Drawing on Kapur and Bielaczyc (2012), the article describes four design principles for the PF problem-solving phase: the problem should be "complex and open to various solutions" (Problem/task); students explore "intuitive solution ideas to this problem by using their prior knowledge" (Activity); exploration is fostered by small-group collaboration (Participation structure) without instructional support, so students can independently explore solution ideas (Social surround). The article contrasts these with the DI phase, which fulfills none of them.
requirements: A complex, novel problem open to multiple solutions; small-group collaboration; no instructional support during problem solving
constraints: Applies to the initial problem-solving phase of PF, not to the subsequent instruction phase
target_learners: secondary school students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry practices, e.g. evaluating causal versus correlational evidence
examples: Students in small groups explored a violence-in-media correlation problem before receiving instruction on the canonical solution
key_sources: Valentina Nachtigall, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Investigating students' perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09556-3

article_title: Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure
citation: Charleen Brand, Christian Hartmann, Katharina Loibl, Nikol Rummel. (2023). Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09619-7
title: Three preparatory mechanisms account of Productive Failure
description: The article works within the account that PF's instructional effect is rooted in three preparatory mechanisms operating during the problem-solving phase prior to instruction: "prior knowledge activation, awareness of knowledge gaps, and recognition of deep features". Prior knowledge activation is operationalized as the quantity of generated solutions, deep feature recognition as solution quality, and gap awareness as self-reports linked to curiosity. The study tested whether collaboration facilitates each mechanism and thereby mediates conceptual knowledge acquisition, and found no such mediations.
requirements: A problem-solving phase before instruction on a concept students cannot yet solve, with instruction that builds on student-generated solutions
constraints: In this study the mechanisms were not associated with learning scores after instruction, and all preparatory variables showed low descriptive values in both conditions
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of variance (standard deviation) in mathematics
examples: Students generated solutions to a soccer-player reliability problem for 45 minutes, reported gap awareness and curiosity, then received 45 minutes of instruction on variance
key_sources: Charleen Brand, Christian Hartmann, Katharina Loibl, Nikol Rummel. (2023). Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09619-7

article_title: Evidence for a competitive relationship between executive functions and statistical learning
citation: Pedraza, F., Farkas, B. C., Vékony, T., Haesebaert, F., Phelipon, R., Mihalecz, I., Janacsek, K., Anders, R., Tillmann, B., Plancher, G. & Németh, D. (2024). Evidence for a competitive relationship between executive functions and statistical learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00243-9
title: PFC-mediated competition model of declarative-procedural interactions: prefrontal executive functions arbitrate against model-free statistical learning
description: The article interprets its results within the interactive memory systems framework, in which learning relies on either the basal ganglia-based procedural system or the medial temporal lobe-based declarative system, with "Larger reliance on one implies a smaller reliance on the other". It focuses on indirect cross-inhibition via prefrontal control processes, proposing that procedural, model-free learning is the 'default' learner overridden by PFC control involvement. The observed negative EF–SL correlations are attributed to "the suppression of model-free, procedural learning by prefrontal EF".
requirements: Requires the assumption that implicit statistical learning taps the procedural, model-free system and that executive functions reflect prefrontal control
constraints: The article states the alternative explanation that both working memory and fluency relate to long-term memory access "needs to be validated through studies that examine long-term memory access, cognitive control, and predictive processes... within a single experimental design"
The EF battery was incomplete: for set shifting and inhibition only the BCST and GNG tasks were available
examples: The two experiments operationalized competition as negative correlations between ASRT learning scores and EF factor scores extracted by maximum-likelihood exploratory factor analysis
key_sources: Pedraza, F., Farkas, B. C., Vékony, T., Haesebaert, F., Phelipon, R., Mihalecz, I., Janacsek, K., Anders, R., Tillmann, B., Plancher, G. & Németh, D. (2024). Evidence for a competitive relationship between executive functions and statistical learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00243-9

article_title: What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks
citation: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1
title: Preparation for Future Collaboration (PFC): a three-phase productive-failure design with phase-specific cognitive mechanisms
description: Preparation for Future Collaboration adapts Productive Failure by splitting exploration into two phases. As the article states, "there are three phases of activity in the PFC design: (1) individual exploration, (2) continued exploration in peer collaboration, and (3) explicit instruction by a teacher." Individual exploration activates prior knowledge and attends to critical features; collaboration engages explaining, elaboration, differentiation, and early knowledge assembly; explicit instruction supports consolidation and assembly of canonical knowledge. The article uses this design as the setting in which micro-failures were observed.
requirements: An exploratory generation task prior to formal instruction, followed by teacher-led explicit instruction presenting canonical concepts
constraints: Cognitive mechanisms engaged during collaboration are inferred; the article notes mechanisms are the same as in productive failure but distributed differently across PFC phases
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of canonical concepts (e.g., the four R's of waste reduction)
examples: The prior study implemented PFC in two fourth-grade classes: individual question items on the four R's, partner collaboration to reach joint decisions, then explicit teacher instruction on the four R's
key_sources: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1

article_title: DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course
citation: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6
title: Depth of search and availability of solution as mechanisms explaining PF's advantage over active learning
description: The authors' explanatory account of why PF outperformed AL when both conditions were active. Building on Loibl et al.'s mechanisms (prior knowledge activation, awareness of knowledge gaps, recognition of deep features), they "attribute the difference in learning between conditions in our study to two factors: depth of search and availability of solution." Quick clicker feedback in AL does not give students time to fully understand problem requirements, whereas PF's extended struggle does; and having the canonical solution available in AL may encourage accepting it "at face value" without dissecting its deep structure.
requirements: Both conditions must already provide active learning support for the mechanism account to be needed
constraints: Offered as the authors' interpretation of a quasi-experiment, not a directly tested mechanism
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and recognition of deep features of domain processes
examples: The authors note some evidence that self-generated feedback during PF's first phase may support better learning than only external feedback
key_sources: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6

article_title: Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits
citation: Vyshedskiy, A., Venkatesh, R., Khokhlovich, E. & Satik, D. (2024). Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00284-0
title: Prefrontal Synthesis (PFS), Prefrontal Modification (PFM), and memory recall as the neurological mechanisms underlying the three language-comprehension clusters
description: The article proposes that the three empirically-derived clusters map onto three neurologically distinct mechanisms. Prefrontal Synthesis (PFS), mediated by the LPFC via frontoposterior connections such as the arcuate fasciculus, deliberately juxtaposes two or more mental objects and underlies the syntactic mechanism. The mechanism of modifying color or size of a single mental object is called "Prefrontal Modification or PFM", limited to the ventral pathway's control of a single object's appearance, and underlies the modifier mechanism. Command comprehension relies only on recalling existing object-encoding neuronal ensembles from memory. The article reports that all seven sentence types requiring combination of two or more mental objects clustered into the syntactic mechanism, "This prediction was borne out of data".
requirements: Interpretation of the clusters depends on the cognitive-neuroscience account linking abilities to PFS, PFM, and memory recall; without defining these subcomponents of symbolic thinking the authors state they could not interpret the clusters
constraints: PFM and PFS are voluntary and deliberate, LPFC-dependent; involuntary imagination and spontaneous insight (vmPFC-dependent) are too slow to mediate comprehension, per the authors
Routinization offers an additional PFS-independent route to interpreting syntactic sentences
target_learners: children and adolescents with language comprehension deficits
target_learning_goals: language comprehension of commands, modifiers, and syntactic structures
examples: Sentences with spatial prepositions, flexible syntax, stories, fairy tales, explanations, possessive pronouns, and verb tenses clustered together as predicted for PFS-mediated types
Understanding "give me the short blue pencil" was interpreted as PFM: recall of the pencil followed by LPFC modification of size and color
key_sources: Vyshedskiy, A., Venkatesh, R., Khokhlovich, E. & Satik, D. (2024). Three mechanisms of language comprehension are revealed through cluster analysis of individuals with language deficits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00284-0

article_title: Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools
citation: Marianthi Grizioti. (2025). Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10477-y
title: PFO model of progressive engagement: Play, Focused Modifications, Open Modifications & Design
description: The PFO model adapts the Use-Modify-Create model for game-based learning, structuring student engagement with a digital game through "layered structural access" to game elements. In the first layer students play the game with access only to its interface; in the second they access and modify certain elements such as a database without making major changes; in the third they access complex functionalities for open modifications or creating a new game. The article reports this scaffolding enabled evolution from micro-level to macro-level computational reasoning.
requirements: Activities must be sequenced across the three layers with progressively deeper access to game structure
constraints: The article notes students struggled in prior UMC research with the transition from Modify to Create, and this study was limited by restricted time for open modifications
target_learners: middle school students with little game design experience
target_learning_goals: progressive development of complex CT practices
examples: Students first played CT-Chef repeatedly to improve scores, then made focused modifications such as changing an ending condition, then created new game versions with added rules, choices and attributes
key_sources: Marianthi Grizioti. (2025). Computational thinking beyond coding: exploring student computational practices while playing and modifying a socio-scientific simulation game with integrated computational tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10477-y

article_title: Evaluation of the Effectiveness of Psychological First Aid Training for Community Nurses in China: A Quasi-Experimental Study on Knowledge and Skills Enhancement.
citation: He Yazhou, Ding Yulan, Yan Jiaqin, Xiong Xiaoning, Huang Shan, Li Sijian. (2026). Evaluation of the Effectiveness of Psychological First Aid Training for Community Nurses in China: A Quasi‐Experimental Study on Knowledge and Skills Enhancement. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70497
title: A 27-item self-report questionnaire measuring PFA knowledge, attitudes, and skills of community nurses
description: The study's instrument comprises 24 scored items plus three open-ended questions: 10 single-choice knowledge items, 6 attitude items and 8 skill items rated on 5-point Likert scales. Content was developed from WHO guidelines, the IASC guidelines, and prior literature. The article reports validation figures: "The scale‐level content validity index (S‐CVI) ... was 0.989, indicating excellent content validity", test–retest reliability with "an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.877", and "a Cronbach's alpha of 0.915". Completion was designed to take 10–15 min and was administered online via WeChat at three time points.
requirements: Seven PFA-experienced experts for content validation
An online platform (WeChat) for administration and SPSS for analysis
constraints: Outcomes are self-reported, which the authors note may include misreporting bias
target_learning_goals: Assessment of PFA knowledge, attitudes, and skills
examples: Test–retest reliability was assessed using responses from 14 nurses who completed the questionnaire twice with a two-week interval
key_sources: He Yazhou, Ding Yulan, Yan Jiaqin, Xiong Xiaoning, Huang Shan, Li Sijian. (2026). Evaluation of the Effectiveness of Psychological First Aid Training for Community Nurses in China: A Quasi‐Experimental Study on Knowledge and Skills Enhancement. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70497

article_title: Validation of a didactic model evaluating the usability, usefulness and acceptability of psychological first aid teaching through simulation.
citation: Saguin Emeric, Salomé Julia, Favodon Benoît, Lahutte Bertrand, Gignoux-Froment Frédérique. (2024). Validation of a didactic model evaluating the usability, usefulness and acceptability of psychological first aid teaching through simulation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06491-y
title: PFA-O introductory simulation training module (French Armed Forces Health Service, 2018)
description: A three-hour Psychological First Aid in Operations module developed by the French Armed Forces Health Service in 2018, "conducted by a nurse and a psychologist working in tandem", aiming to develop basic skills in groups of around ten military trainees as part of operational preparation. Sessions comprise one hour of theoretical training followed by two hours of practical training including three successive relational simulations. Trainers credited the teaching with strengthening interpersonal skills (76.27%) and identification of people in psychological distress (72.88%), and 81.13% felt it was well received by trainees’ units.
requirements: Delivery requires a nurse and a psychologist trained as PFA-O trainers working in tandem
constraints: Designed for and evaluated within the French military population in an institutional setting with substantial material resources
target_learners: Military personnel in operational preparation, in groups of around ten trainees
target_learning_goals: Basic psychological first aid skills: identifying signs of psychological suffering, adapting the caregiving relationship, and guiding early referral to care
examples: The module was evaluated by 59 trainers using the 15-criterion didactic model, with 76.27% of respondents having conducted at least one introductory session
key_sources: Saguin Emeric, Salomé Julia, Favodon Benoît, Lahutte Bertrand, Gignoux-Froment Frédérique. (2024). Validation of a didactic model evaluating the usability, usefulness and acceptability of psychological first aid teaching through simulation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06491-y

article_title: Assessment of the level of agreement in the interpretation of plain radiographs of lumbar spondylosis among clinical physiotherapists in Ghana.
citation: Bello Ajediran I, Ofori Eric K, Alabi Oluwasegun J, Adjei David N. (2014). Assessment of the level of agreement in the interpretation of plain radiographs of lumbar spondylosis among clinical physiotherapists in Ghana. BMC Medical Imaging. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3986614/
title: 24-point radiograph interpretation assessment guide validated with radiologists (Cronbach's alpha 0.79)
description: An assessment guide developed from an experienced independent radiologist's identification of pathological features on three plain film radiographs of lumbar spondylosis, listing "A total of 24 features were identified by the radiologist from three PFR with each consisting 8 features". Correct identification scores 1 point, wrong or non-identification 0, with total scores of 0–8, 9–16, and 17–24 interpreted as low, moderate, and high agreement. Test–retest reliability among seven experienced radiologists yielded "A good internal consistency of 0.79 Chrombach's alpha value". The guide served as the gold standard for scoring physiotherapists in the survey.
requirements: An experienced independent radiologist to establish the gold-standard feature list for the selected radiographs
constraints: Developed from only three plain film radiographs of lumbar spondylosis, which the authors state limits the study's external validity
target_learning_goals: Correct identification of pathological features on plain film radiographs of lumbar spondylosis
examples: Physiotherapists viewed the three radiographs and listed identifiable patho-anatomical features, scored 1 point per correct feature against the guide
key_sources: Bello Ajediran I, Ofori Eric K, Alabi Oluwasegun J, Adjei David N. (2014). Assessment of the level of agreement in the interpretation of plain radiographs of lumbar spondylosis among clinical physiotherapists in Ghana. BMC Medical Imaging. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3986614/
